prompt: Who was Sir Āpirana Ngata and why is he significant?

response.response_text:
Sir Āpirana Turupa Ngata (1874–1950) was one of the most influential Māori leaders of the 20th century — a politician, scholar, cultural champion, and reformer whose work shaped the course of Māori history in Aotearoa New Zealand. His biographer, Ranginui Walker, described him as "a man of such extraordinary gifts of intelligence, energy and foresight" that among his own Ngāti Porou tribe he was esteemed as a god among men. [[1]](cite://1/1)

## Early Life and Education

Ngata was born on 3 July 1874 at Te Araroa on the East Coast, with connections to the leaders of Ngāti Porou. [[2]](cite://2/1) His father, Paratene Ngata, was a storekeeper, progressive farmer, Native Land Court assessor, and expert in tribal lore, while his paternal great-uncle Rāpata Wahawaha had led Ngāti Porou troops on the side of the Crown during the wars of the 1860s. [[2]](cite://2/2) Both men profoundly influenced Āpirana, who followed their policy of loyalty to the Crown throughout his life. [[2]](cite://2/3)

His family was insistent that he be educated in Pākehā learning and skills so that he could turn them to the benefit of Ngāti Porou and the Māori people. [[2]](cite://2/4) He became the first Māori to graduate from a New Zealand university, completing a Bachelor of Arts in political science and, three years later, a law degree. [[3]](cite://3/1) Rather than practising law, however, he threw himself into reforming the social and economic situation of Māori. [[4]](cite://4/1) As a qualified lawyer his mana (prestige) rose enormously, and from 1899 he was sought after at hui (gatherings) throughout the country. [[4]](cite://4/2)

## Political Career

In 1905, Ngata won the Eastern Māori parliamentary seat, which he would hold until 1943, eventually becoming "father" of the House. [[5]](cite://5/1) He was a superb parliamentarian — a skilled debater who could fill the parliamentary galleries whenever he rose to speak. [[5]](cite://5/2)

During this long career he assisted in drafting crucial legislation, including the Native Land Act 1909, and served on the 1907–08 Native Land Commission, which was critical of the government's use of pre-emption to purchase Māori land below value. [[5]](cite://5/3) In December 1928 he became native minister in the United Party government, ranked third in cabinet and occasionally acting as deputy prime minister. [[6]](cite://6/1) He held that office until 1934. [[7]](cite://7/1)

His parliamentary career finally ended in 1943 when he was defeated by the Rātana Labour candidate, Tiaki Ōmana. Even after leaving Parliament, he remained influential as an elder statesman, coaching successive ministers of Māori affairs. [[8]](cite://8/1)

## Land Development

Ngata's most transformative practical work was in Māori land development. Until the late 1920s, Māori struggled to develop their land as they were not eligible for farm assistance programmes. [[9]](cite://9/1) As native minister, Ngata secured government funding and spearheaded large-scale development schemes — clearing, grassing, and stocking tribal land across the country, providing employment for thousands of Māori during the Depression. [[10]](cite://10/1) By 1939, land development was employing around 5,000 Māori. [[11]](cite://11/1)

He also established the Waiapu Farmers Co-operative Company in 1912, partly to give Ngāti Porou access to credit, and promoted dairying on the Waiapu valley flats in the 1920s. [[12]](cite://12/1) His success was largely due to his experience of farming on the East Coast combined with his knowledge of European law. [[13]](cite://13/1)

A 1934 commission of inquiry found that he and his supervisors had been careless about accounting for state funds, and that some staff were corrupt. Ngata accepted full responsibility and resigned from cabinet. [[10]](cite://10/2) Despite this setback, his land development legacy endured — the Labour government that followed carried on his schemes with even greater expenditure. [[8]](cite://8/2)

## Cultural Renaissance

Alongside his political and economic work, Ngata led a remarkable renaissance in Māori knowledge and culture. [[14]](cite://14/1) He was a passionate champion of carving and the decorative arts, of Māori music, dance and haka, of poetry and linguistic traditions, seeing large building projects such as meeting houses and churches as a way to showcase "the heirlooms of the ancestors." [[15]](cite://15/1)

He established the Board of Māori Ethnological Research in 1923 and the Māori Purposes Fund Control Board in 1924, using their resources to support the Polynesian Society and its publications. [[16]](cite://16/1) He also initiated a publishing programme that included his own annotated collection of Māori waiata (songs), *Ngā Mōteatea*, and oversaw the building of carved meeting houses throughout the country. [[14]](cite://14/2)

In 1918, Ngata wrote to the Minister of Internal Affairs urging that specialists be sent into the field to record Māori songs, oratory, and village life — including the filming of haka and pois — recognising that Māori culture had embedded its wisdom and history in spoken language rather than literature. [[17]](cite://17/1) He also inspired the building of St Mary's Church at Tikitiki in the 1920s as a memorial to Ngāti Porou who died in World War I, blending Māori and Pākehā design. [[18]](cite://18/1)

## War Service and Legacy

During World War I, Ngata worked with other Māori MPs to recruit Māori troops and agitated to have them grouped into a Māori battalion after the disaster of Gallipoli. [[19]](cite://19/1) He is remembered as "the father of the Māori Battalion." [[20]](cite://20/1) He also supported the formation of the 28 (Māori) Battalion in World War II. [[21]](cite://21/1)

Ngata died on 14 July 1950, leaving an enduring legacy as a vital contributor to the early 20th-century Māori revival through land development, cultural preservation, and identity maintenance. [[22]](cite://22/1) He is recognised as the father of biculturalism in New Zealand [[3]](cite://3/2) and his portrait appears on the New Zealand $50 note. [[23]](cite://23/1) The inscription on his memorial beside St Mary's Church declares him "the vine which bound together the churches and tribes of the Māori people; the pillar of Māori traditions and the guiding star of his people." [[24]](cite://24/1)
